what_it_does: Training a large neural network involves distributing the work across dozens or hundreds of chips that must constantly share updated values — a step called collective communication (for example, averaging gradients across all chips at once, called all-reduce). Current wafer-scale designs (where many chips are manufactured on one very large silicon wafer and wired together) use a simple 2D grid of connections, which forces different types of parallelism — dividing the model by layers (pipeline parallelism), by the model's internal dimensions (tensor parallelism), and by data batches (data parallelism) — to fight over the same wires. FRED introduces tiny programmable switching points embedded in the wafer's interconnect fabric, forming a flexible network that can be reconfigured so each parallelism dimension gets its own non-overlapping communication paths. Additionally, the switches themselves can participate in the summation operation, reducing how much data flows through the network overall.
